title: “SUCH WERE SOME OF YOU”—THE FIVE WORDS SATAN NEVER WANTED YOU TO READ AFTER PAUL’S LIST OF SEXUAL SINS
paragraphs: “SUCH WERE SOME OF YOU”—THE FIVE WORDS SATAN NEVER WANTED YOU TO READ AFTER PAUL’S LIST OF SEXUAL SINS
First came the sins nobody wanted exposed. Then came a sentence nobody expected. And hidden between those two realities is the Gospel that can turn your deepest scandal into a testimony of grace.
There is a terrifying way to read the Bible.
You can read just enough to feel condemned… and stop one verse before discovering what Jesus Christ has done for sinners.
Imagine someone sitting alone at two in the morning.
The room is dark. The phone is still glowing. The search history has already been erased.
Another promise has been broken.
Another temptation has won.
Another prayer sounds painfully familiar.
“Lord, I'm sorry. I said I wouldn't do this again.”
Maybe it was pornography.
Maybe an affair.
Maybe a sexual relationship that crossed boundaries you once promised God you would never cross.
Maybe a secret addiction, a pattern of lust, or a relationship that has slowly pulled your heart away from obedience to Christ.

Or perhaps your struggle has nothing to do with sex. Perhaps it is greed, drunkenness, deception, bitterness, or the quiet pride that makes you feel morally superior to people whose sins are more visible than yours.
Whatever the struggle, you know the feeling.
That terrible distance between the person you appear to be and the person you fear you have become.
You still know the worship songs.
You still know how to say “God bless you.”
You might even serve in church.
But somewhere inside, a question keeps returning.
If people knew everything about me, would they still believe I belong to Jesus?
And then you open your Bible to 1 Corinthians 6.
Paul begins naming sins.
Sexual immorality.
Idolatry.
Adultery.
Men who engage in same-sex sexual acts.
Theft.
Greed.
Drunkenness.
Verbal abuse.
Swindling.
And suddenly, the passage no longer feels like something written to an ancient church.
It feels painfully close.
Paul warns that those characterized by such unrighteousness will not inherit the kingdom of God.
He does not soften the warning.
He does not call darkness light.
He does not suggest that God's grace makes repentance unnecessary.
And for a moment, the weight of those words is almost unbearable.
But please…
Do not close your Bible at verse 10.
Because verse 11 contains one of the most astonishing declarations ever written to people with sinful pasts.
“And such were some of you.”
Five words in the familiar English phrasing.
A lifetime of shame confronted by the power of the Gospel.
And a truth that changes everything.
The apostle Paul was writing to real believers in Corinth, a city shaped by the religious, commercial, and sexual practices of the Greco-Roman world.
These were not imaginary people in a theological illustration.
They were men and women with histories.
Some had worshiped idols.
Some had exploited others.
Some had committed sexual sins.
Some had been controlled by destructive desires.
Some had lived in patterns of behavior that contradicted the holiness of God.
And yet Paul addressed the Corinthian congregation as people called to belong to Jesus Christ.
How?
Not because their sins had never happened.
Not because their past was suddenly harmless.
Not because God had decided holiness no longer mattered.
But because something greater than their past had entered their lives.
Jesus Christ had saved them.
Listen to the passage in its original Greek.
“Καὶ ταῦτά τινες ἦτε· ἀλλὰ ἀπελούσασθε, ἀλλὰ ἡγιάσθητε, ἀλλὰ ἐδικαιώθητε ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι τοῦ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ καὶ ἐν τῷ πνεύματι τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν.”
— 1 Corinthians 6:11
A careful English rendering is:
“And such were some of you. But you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”
Notice the first part.
Καὶ ταῦτά τινες ἦτε — Kai tauta tines ēte.
“And such were some of you.”
The Greek verb ἦτε (ēte) is an imperfect form of the verb “to be,” referring here to what some of them formerly were.
Paul was not saying that their sins had been imaginary.
He was not denying their history.
He was acknowledging it.
Some of you really lived this way.
Some of you really practiced these things.
Some of you really were caught in those patterns.
But then comes a word that changes the direction of the sentence.
ἀλλά — alla.
BUT.
It is a small Greek word carrying an enormous contrast.
You were this.
But.
You lived that way.
But.
You were guilty.
But.
You were not beyond the saving power of Jesus Christ.
That little word does not erase God's judgment against sin.
It announces that God's saving grace has intervened.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear that distinction.
Your past may explain some of your wounds.
It may explain why trust is difficult.
It may explain the consequences you still carry.
It may even explain why certain temptations remain painfully familiar.
But for those who belong to Christ, the past does not possess the final authority to define their standing before God.
Jesus does.
Now consider what Paul says next.
“But you were washed.”
The Greek word is ἀπελούσασθε (apelousasthe), from a verb meaning to wash off or wash away.

Its form is middle voice, so it should not be treated as though the Greek grammar alone proves a simple passive statement. Nevertheless, within Paul's sentence, the cleansing is inseparable from the saving work of Christ and the Spirit of God.
Paul is describing something far deeper than improving one's reputation.
He is speaking of cleansing from sin.
Think about that.
There are stains no amount of public success can remove.
You can move to another city.
Change your phone number.
Delete old conversations.
Start a new relationship.
Build a new career.
Become admired by people who know nothing about your history.
And still carry guilt that follows you into every quiet room.
Because the deepest problem of sin is not merely that someone might discover it.
The deepest problem is that sin is committed before a holy God.
And no amount of hiding can cleanse the conscience.
That is why the Gospel is such extraordinary news.
The blood of Jesus Christ accomplishes what our self-improvement never could.
First John 1:7 declares that the blood of Jesus cleanses us from all sin.
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because Christ's sacrifice is sufficient.
Jesus did not come merely to teach guilty people how to appear respectable.
He came to save sinners.
He lived the righteous life we failed to live.
He died for sins He did not commit.
He bore the judgment sinners deserve.
And He rose from the dead, victorious over sin and death.
That is why forgiveness is not God pretending evil never happened.
Forgiveness is mercy grounded in the finished work of Jesus Christ.
And perhaps the person who needs to hear that most is the person who has been trying to punish themselves long after confessing their sin.
You replay the memory.
You hate what you did.
You wonder whether God is tired of hearing your prayers.
But self-condemnation cannot accomplish what only Christ can accomplish.
There is a difference between godly sorrow that leads to repentance and hopeless shame that tells you there is no way home.
Second Corinthians 7:10 speaks of godly grief producing repentance that leads to salvation.
The Holy Spirit convicts us of sin so that we turn toward God.
Despair tells us to remain hidden.
Grace calls us into the light.
And then Paul continues.
“But you were sanctified.”
The Greek is ἡγιάσθητε (hēgiasthēte).
It means “you were sanctified,” or set apart as holy.
This is not merely a promise that one day, after years of effort, God might finally consider you His.
Paul is describing a decisive work of God in those who have come to Christ.
They have been set apart for Him.
And this new belonging carries a new calling.
Because grace does not simply forgive the sinner while leaving sin enthroned.
Grace brings us into a new relationship with God, in which we are called to grow in holiness.
This matters especially when discussing sexual sin.
The Bible does not teach that sexual desire itself makes a person filthy.
Nor does it teach that a person who experiences temptation has automatically committed every sin they are tempted to commit.
Scripture distinguishes temptation from sinful action, and calls believers to resist temptation through the power and grace of God.
But Scripture also refuses to treat sexual conduct as morally meaningless.
Paul's warning in 1 Corinthians 6 is serious because our bodies matter to God.
A few verses later, he tells believers that their bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit and that they have been bought with a price.
Therefore, they are to glorify God in their bodies.
That means following Jesus involves more than claiming a Christian identity while deliberately protecting a lifestyle of disobedience.
It means surrendering our desires, choices, relationships, and bodies to the Lord who redeemed us.
And surrender can be costly.
Sometimes it means ending a relationship that continually leads you into sin.
Sometimes it means confessing deception.
Sometimes it means seeking pastoral care, accountability, or professional help for compulsive behavior.
Sometimes it means making restitution.
Sometimes it means accepting consequences instead of demanding that forgiveness erase them.
And sometimes it means waking up the next morning and choosing obedience again, even though yesterday's temptation has not magically disappeared.
Sanctification does not mean a believer never struggles. It means sin is no longer something we are called to defend as our master.
Romans 6 teaches that those united with Christ are no longer to let sin reign in their mortal bodies.
This does not promise instant freedom from every temptation.
But it does proclaim a new allegiance.
You do not have to make peace with the very thing Christ calls you to forsake.
And you do not have to believe that a difficult struggle makes obedience impossible.
The same Lord who commands holiness also gives grace to help His people pursue it.
Then comes Paul's third declaration.
“But you were justified.”
The Greek word is ἐδικαιώθητε (edikaiōthēte).
It means “you were justified.”
This is courtroom language.
It concerns being declared righteous before God.
And this is where the Gospel becomes almost too beautiful for a guilty conscience to comprehend.
Imagine standing before a judge who knows everything.
Every hidden motive.
Every private betrayal.
Every secret compromise.
Every lie you convinced yourself was necessary.
Every moment when you knew what was right and deliberately chose otherwise.
There is no missing evidence.
No technical loophole.
No successful performance.
You cannot argue that your good deeds have somehow canceled your guilt.
And then the Gospel announces that righteousness before God is received through faith in Jesus Christ.
Not earned by moral achievement.
Not purchased by religious donations.
Not secured by a spotless personal history.
Christ Himself is the Savior.
Romans 3:23–24 declares that all have sinned and fall short of God's glory, and that justification is by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.
That includes the sexually immoral person who repents.
The greedy person who repents.
The proud person who repents.
The religious hypocrite who repents.
And the person who spent years believing that everyone else was too sinful to deserve the mercy they themselves desperately needed.
At the foot of the cross, nobody gets to boast.
The person with a publicly scandalous past cannot save themselves.
And the person with a respectable reputation cannot save themselves either.
We are not rescued because our sins were small. We are rescued because our Savior is great.
But there is something else we must understand about Paul's list.
It is often read as though Paul were only interested in condemning sexual sin.
He was not.
Sexual immorality and adultery are there.
The Greek terms μαλακοί (malakoi) and ἀρσενοκοῖται (arsenokoitai) also appear in verse 9.
These terms deserve careful treatment.

Malakoi literally means “soft ones,” and its meaning depends on context. In this vice list, it is often understood as referring to males associated with certain sexual practices, though its precise scope is debated.

Arsenokoitai is a rare compound built from words meaning “male” and “bed,” and is widely understood by traditional Christian interpreters as referring to male same-sex sexual activity. Scholars continue to debate its exact historical scope and the best English rendering.
It would be irresponsible to pretend these translation questions do not exist.
It would also be irresponsible to erase Paul's moral argument simply because parts of the vocabulary are difficult.

The larger passage places sexual conduct under the lordship of Christ, and traditional Christian interpretation understands Paul's teaching in continuity with the biblical sexual ethic expressed elsewhere in Scripture.
But notice something essential.
Paul does not isolate one group of sinners and declare everyone else morally superior.
He includes thieves.
Greedy people.
Drunkards.
Those who verbally abuse others.
Those who defraud others.
And elsewhere in Scripture, pride, hatred, envy, hypocrisy, and countless other sins are condemned.
This passage gives nobody permission to mock, harass, dehumanize, or mistreat another person.
Every human being bears God's image and deserves dignity.
And every human being needs God's mercy.
The church must never become a place where certain sins are publicly condemned while other sins are privately celebrated.
The businessman who cheats people cannot hide behind his respectable suit.
The church leader who manipulates others cannot hide behind his microphone.
The married person committing adultery cannot hide behind a wedding ring.
The person filled with contempt cannot hide behind theological vocabulary.
And the believer who condemns everyone else's failures while refusing to repent of their own has not understood the warning.
Paul begins verse 9 with a command that should make all of us examine ourselves.
“Do not be deceived.”
The warning is not an invitation to obsess over someone else's sins.
It is an invitation to stop lying to ourselves about our own.
And still, the passage does not end with the warning.
It ends with grace.
That is the extraordinary thing.
Paul could have written a letter that simply reminded the Corinthians how terrible their former lives had been.
Instead, he reminded them what Christ had done.
“Such were some of you.”
Not “such were all of you,” because Paul was not claiming every Corinthian believer had committed every listed sin.
Not “such are you forever,” because he was addressing people whose lives had been changed through Christ.
And not “such were some of you, therefore you can never be tempted again.”
The Corinthians still needed correction.
The very existence of this letter proves that believers can struggle with serious sin and need serious rebuke.
But their failures were not a reason to abandon the Gospel.
They were a reason to return to its truth.
That distinction may save someone from two equally destructive lies.
The first lie says, “God is gracious, so my sin does not matter.”
The second says, “My sin is terrible, so God's grace cannot reach me.”
Both misunderstand the cross.
The cross reveals how serious sin really is.
And the cross reveals how astonishing God's mercy really is.
Jesus did not die so that we could comfortably remain enslaved to the sins that destroy us.
He died and rose so that sinners could be forgiven, reconciled to God, and brought into new life.
And perhaps this is where the story becomes personal.
Because there is a difference between believing that Jesus forgives sinners and believing that Jesus can forgive you.
You can preach grace to everyone else while secretly believing that your own history is the exception.
You can tell a struggling friend that God is merciful, then spend the night wondering whether you have exhausted that mercy.
You can sing about the blood of Jesus while still living as though your shame is more powerful than His sacrifice.
But hear the Gospel.
Christ did not wait for sinners to become clean before coming to save them.
Romans 5:8 says God demonstrated His love for us in that Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
And when Jesus called people to follow Him, He did not invite them to continue unchanged.
He called them to repentance and faith.
Think of the woman caught in adultery in John 8, a passage whose manuscript history is disputed and which is absent from some of the earliest surviving manuscripts.
In the familiar account, Jesus refuses to join the crowd in condemning her, yet also tells her to leave her life of sin.
Mercy and holiness are not enemies.
Or think of the Samaritan woman in John 4.
Jesus knew her complicated relational history.
He did not need her to manufacture a respectable story before speaking to her about living water.
And the conversation led her to tell others about Him.
Or think of the apostle Paul himself.
Before becoming a messenger of the Gospel, he persecuted the church.
Later, he called himself the foremost of sinners in 1 Timothy 1:15–16, pointing to Christ's mercy as an example of His patience.
The man who wrote “such were some of you” knew something about a past that could not be undone.
He had memories.
He had a history.
He had reasons to be humbled.
But he also had a Savior.
And that is the heart of our message at Gospel Warrior.
Not because Jesus makes the past disappear.
Not because repentance cancels every earthly consequence.
Not because faith guarantees that every damaged relationship will be restored exactly as it was.
But because Jesus can redeem a life that sin has wounded.
He can forgive what you cannot undo.
He can transform what you thought would always control you.
He can teach you to walk in truth after years of hiding.
He can give you a new purpose even when your old mistakes still cast shadows.
And He can turn the testimony of a forgiven sinner into an invitation for someone else to come home.
That is not a promise that every Christian story will be easy.
Some believers still face painful consequences from former choices.
Some still battle temptations.
Some carry wounds caused by other people's sins.
And some need years of wise counsel, healing, accountability, and patient discipleship.
The Gospel does not require us to pretend those realities are simple.
It gives us hope in the middle of them.
Because our confidence is not in the speed of our recovery.
Our confidence is in the faithfulness of Jesus Christ.
Maybe you are reading this while hiding something.
Maybe your marriage is strained because of a betrayal.
Maybe you are exhausted by a habit you keep promising to stop.
Maybe you are afraid to ask for help because you have built an image of spiritual strength that nobody is allowed to question.
Maybe you have been wounded by people who used Scripture as a weapon rather than speaking truth with love.
Or maybe you are the person who has spent years pointing at the sins of others because you are terrified to confront your own.
Wherever you are, the invitation is not to manufacture another religious performance.
It is to come honestly before Christ.
Confess your sin.
Turn from it.
Believe the Gospel.
Seek the help you need.
Make what amends you can without demanding that others immediately trust you.
And continue following Jesus, one obedient step at a time.
First John 1:9 teaches that when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us from unrighteousness.
And Romans 8:1 declares that there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
Those promises are not excuses for deliberate rebellion.
They are anchors for repentant sinners who trust in Christ.
You may still remember who you were.
But if you are in Christ, do not forget what He has done.
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
Not three trophies for people who managed to save themselves.
Three declarations pointing to the grace of God.
What is the one area of your life where you need to stop hiding and begin surrendering?

You do not have to publish your most intimate sins in a public comment section. Some confessions belong in private conversations with a trusted pastor, counselor, or mature believer who can respond wisely and protect your dignity.
Or, if you are struggling and need the encouragement of fellow believers, simply write:
And if the Lord has already carried you through a season of repentance and restoration, consider sharing a brief testimony of His faithfulness.
Someone reading the comments may be struggling with the very thing God has helped you face.
Your words could remind that person they are not alone.
And please, think of one person who needs to read this.
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Not someone you want to expose.
Someone you love.
Someone who has been quietly withdrawing from fellowship.
Someone who thinks they have sinned too much.
Someone who has mistaken shame for repentance.
Someone who desperately needs to understand that the Gospel does not end at the list of sins.
If this ministry has helped you grow, I also want to invite you into something deeper.
Our desire is to help build a community of people who take Scripture seriously, love Jesus deeply, encourage one another honestly, and refuse to surrender their lives to spiritual complacency.
These resources are part of our commitment to making biblical encouragement and Christian learning accessible.
I want to be careful about something, though.
You do not have to pay for God's favor.
But voluntary support for Gospel ministry is a legitimate and beautiful expression of Christian generosity.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
And Philippians 4:15–17 shows how believers supported Paul's ministry and shared in its work.
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not guilt.
Not pressure.
Not a promise that money will make God love you more.
But the opportunity to participate in making Christ-centered encouragement and discipleship resources available to more people.
These items can be reminders of biblical truth, encouragement for daily life, or gifts that open meaningful conversations about Jesus.
It is the opportunity to help more people encounter the message of Christ.
You can glorify God through many forms of faithful service. Financial support is one possible expression, never a requirement for belonging to Christ.
If you are unable to give financially, please do not feel excluded.
You are welcome here.
Read the Scriptures.
Use the free resources.
Grow in your faith.
Encourage others.
And help carry the message of Jesus Christ into places our page may never reach on its own.
It is about people.
Real people.
People with hidden struggles.
People carrying regret.
People who have spent years believing that God has no use for someone with their history.
People who need to hear that repentance is possible, forgiveness is real, and new life is found in Jesus Christ.
And that brings us back to the words Paul wrote nearly two thousand years ago.
“And such were some of you.”
Read them slowly.
Not as permission to romanticize the past.
Not as a guarantee that everyone who identifies as Christian has genuinely turned to Christ.
Not as an excuse to ignore Paul's warning.
But as a testimony to what the Lord Jesus Christ and the Spirit of God can do in the lives of sinners.
The church in Corinth was not a museum of flawless people.
It was a community called to holiness by the Savior who had rescued them.
And the church today should never forget that.
We are not called to celebrate sin.
We are not called to crush the repentant.
We are not called to pretend holiness is optional.
We are called to proclaim Jesus Christ, crucified and risen, who saves sinners and transforms lives.
So if you are still hiding, come into the light.
If you are defending sin, repent.
If you are drowning in shame, look to Christ.
If you are exhausted by the struggle, seek help and keep following Him.
If you have been forgiven, extend mercy without compromising truth.
And if you have been restored, never forget the grace that brought you home.
Because one day, the most astonishing part of your testimony may not be the darkness you once walked through.
It may be the mercy of the Savior who refused to leave you there.
Your past may still remember your name, but it does not get to overrule what Jesus Christ has done.
